title: Great Business Leaders Love the Flywheel
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: This piece challenges the common leadership instinct to treat growth problems as a missing single element, whether a new hire, a new feature, or a new campaign, arguing instead that a business functions as a network of interdependencies where an investment fails not on its own merits but because the surrounding system cannot carry its weight. It builds its central argument around Jim Collins's Flywheel Effect from Good to Great: a heavy wheel that seems to accomplish nothing with early pushes, but compounds momentum once pushes consistently land at the same point rather than being scattered across different initiatives. Amazon's early growth loop, book selection feeding customer experience feeding traffic feeding third-party sellers feeding more selection feeding lower costs, serves as the worked example, with the piece specifically noting that no single move in that loop was clever or hard to copy; what was uncopyable was the compounding loop itself, which only pays out when every part runs together. The piece translates this into a concrete leadership exercise: name your own flywheel, identify what actually produces the next customer and the one after that, and locate the single component quietly throttling the rest of the system. It closes with several supporting quotes from Collins, Rumelt, Godin, Christensen, Anderson and Adams, and Rometty reinforcing the same systems-thinking theme.
points: Reframes the common leadership instinct to diagnose growth problems as a single missing element (a hire, a feature, a campaign) as usually wrong, arguing failures occur because the surrounding system cannot carry the investment's weight.

Uses Amazon's early growth loop (selection to experience to traffic to sellers to selection to lower costs) as a worked example of Jim Collins's Flywheel Effect, specifically noting that no individual move was clever or hard to copy, only the compounding loop was.

Makes the critical mechanical point about flywheels explicit: pushes only compound if they land at the same point in the system; pushing at different points scatters the energy and the process fails to accelerate.

Converts the concept into a concrete leadership exercise: name your own flywheel by asking what actually produces the next customer, then the next, noting most leadership teams have never written this down.
Argues that in almost every business one component is quietly throttling the rest of the system, and that component is rarely the one currently getting the most leadership attention.
quotes: A business is not a group of departments; it is a network of interdependencies. Sales promises what product has yet to deliver. The product roadmap gets impacted by what support hears during the last escalation.

A flywheel is heavy and slow at the start. Every push seems to accomplish nothing. Then the pushes begin to compound, and eventually momentum starts to build. The catch is that the pushes have to land in the same place.

Amazon's loop started with book selection and a great customer experience. A better experience brought more traffic. Traffic attracted third-party sellers. More sellers meant more selection, which improved the experience again.
No single move on that list is clever. A competitor could have copied any one of them. What was hard to copy was the loop because it only pays out when all parts of it are running.

In almost every business, one component is quietly throttling the rest, and it is rarely the one getting the most attention. Fix that part, and everything you have already built starts working harder.
